articles.author: DC
articles.description:
If you’ve ever diffed two CSV exports and gotten a wall of red, only to realize nothing actually changed — you’ve hit the same problem I kept running into.
Most diff tools compare files line by line. That works fine for code, but it falls apart on tabular data the moment a single row gets inserted, deleted, or reordered anywhere in the file. Every row after that point shifts position, and a position-based diff reports all of them as “changed” — even though the underlying data is identical.
Here’s a minimal example of the problem:
id,name,status
id,name,status
The fix: match rows by identity, not position.
I built a diff that detects a likely key column automatically (id, _id, key, slug, code, name — whatever’s actually present) and matches rows across both files by that value instead of line number. Reordering, insertions, and deletions stop generating noise. You see exactly three things: rows added, rows removed, and cells that genuinely changed on a row that exists in both files.
The same principle applies to JSON and XML — array items get matched by a detected key field rather than array index, so reordering an array in an API response doesn’t produce a diff full of false changes either.
That grew into a small toolkit:
• Conversion — JSON↔CSV, JSON↔XML, flatten/unflatten nested structures
• Diffing — JSON, CSV, XML, all key-aware as above
• Schema tooling — generate a JSON Schema from a sample, validate data against one, or render it straight to a TypeScript interface or Zod schema
• Access — a browser tool (nothing uploaded, runs entirely client-side), a CLI (npx recast-cli, works offline), and a GitHub Action for CI

Free tier covers everything above with reasonable size limits — it’s at tryrecast.app if you want to try it on your own data.
Curious whether others have hit this same reordering problem and what you used to work around it — Beyond Compare, a custom script, something else?
Try it: http://tryrecast.app
articles.title: Why your CSV diff tool is lying to you (and how to fix it)

So you're deep in a session with Claude Code or Cursor, everything's flowing, and then it hits a wall:

articles.description:
Every typist hits the same wall. You go from 40 to 55 WPM in a few weeks of casual practice, then you stall. You keep typing every day, the number doesn't move, and the internet's advice ("just practice more") stops working. Here's why, and what actually breaks the plateau.
When people say they're "stuck," they usually mean their peak speed hasn't moved. But peak speed was never the bottleneck - it's how fast you recover from a miss that determines your average.
Watch a 40 WPM typist and an 80 WPM typist type the same paragraph. Their peak keystroke speed in a clean run is often closer than you'd expect. The real gap is what happens after an error: the 40 WPM typist pauses, looks at the screen, backspaces, and restarts the word. The 80 WPM typist's fingers keep moving almost without a brea…

Agentic AI for Production Support: Moving from Alerts to Intelligent Incident Resolution


Production support today is still highly dependent on engineers.
An alert comes in → engineer checks logs → searches previous incidents → identifies possible RCA → validates the solution → takes action.
While working on this problem, I started exploring a simple question:

Incident → Clean Layer → RAG → AI Agent → RCA → Validation → Human Approval → Action
Instead of sending every incident directly to an LLM, the system first prepares and controls the context.
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) searches historical i…

articles.author: WebAZ
articles.description:
AI agents can already search catalogs, compare options, and recommend a product.
That is useful, but it is not commerce.
Commerce begins when the recommendation becomes a commitment:
Who approved the purchase?
Where does the money go?
What state is the order in?
Which product variant and inventory snapshot did the buyer accept?
What evidence survives if fulfillment fails?
How does a return reach the right address?
Most agent demos stop before these questions. WebAZ is an open-source protocol trying to make the messy part after "buy" explicit, inspectable, and usable by both humans and AI agents.
WebAZ now runs two real settlement rails. On neither rail does WebAZ take custody of the principal.
The buyer pays the seller directly, off-platform. WebAZ records the payment-instruction snapshot,…
articles.title: AI Agents Can Find Products. The Hard Part Starts After "Buy."

A convincing AI influencer is not just a good portrait. It is a character that stays recognizable across posts, campaigns, and formats.
That sounds obvious, but most image-generation workflows begin from a blank prompt every time. The result may look impressive in isolation while the face, styling, tone, or audience changes from one asset to the next.
For a reusable virtual creator, continuity has several layers:
Visual identity: facial features, hair, proportions, wardrobe, and recurring details
Creative direction: aesthetic, lighting, locations, and camera language
Voice: personality, vocabulary, and the way the character addresses an audience
Positioning: niche, target audience, and the topics the character should or should not cover
If those details live only inside a long prompt, they…
